sources.name: Scamwatch
sources.organisation: National Anti-Scam Centre, Australian Competition and Consumer Commission

articles.title: Urgency and pressure
articles.summary: Learn why demands to act immediately are a warning sign and how to slow the situation down safely.
articles.overview: Scammers use a deadline, threat or limited-time reward to keep you from checking the story. Genuine organisations may need action, but they should allow you to verify the request through an official channel.
signs: You are told to act before hanging up or before a countdown ends.
The person becomes angry or threatening when you ask questions.
You are discouraged from speaking with family, your bank or the organisation.
actions: Stop the conversation and write down the claim without following supplied links.
Find the organisation's number or app independently and ask whether the request is genuine.
Give yourself time; a legitimate process will explain safe next steps.
recovery: Contact your bank immediately if money or card details were shared.
Change affected account credentials from a trusted device.
Report the approach to Scamwatch and keep non-sensitive evidence.

articles.title: Offers that seem too good to be true
articles.summary: Check prizes, bargains and unexpected investments before emotion or scarcity overrides a careful decision.
articles.overview: A large reward, unusually low price or guaranteed return can be used to make risk feel smaller than it is. The offer may borrow logos, reviews or celebrity images without permission.
signs: You did not enter the competition or request the investment contact.
A fee, tax or deposit is required before receiving the promised benefit.
The seller avoids normal contracts, refunds or independently verifiable details.
actions: Search for the organisation independently and compare the offer with its official site.
Check licence or registration information through the relevant Australian regulator.
Do not pay by gift card, cryptocurrency or an account supplied in private chat.
recovery: Ask your payment provider whether a transfer can be stopped or disputed.
Save the advertisement, account details and receipts without further contact.
Report investment claims to ASIC and other scams to Scamwatch.

articles.title: How to verify a request independently
articles.summary: Use a separate trusted path to confirm who contacted you and what they really need.
articles.overview: Independent verification means not using the phone number, link or contact details supplied in the suspicious message. It breaks the scammer's control over the conversation and lets the real organisation check its own records.
signs: The supplied callback number differs from the organisation's public contact page.
A caller offers to transfer you to a supposedly secure department.
The message says normal support staff will not know about the request.
actions: End the contact and open the official app, statement or bookmarked website yourself.
Explain the claim without sharing codes and ask staff to inspect your account notes.
For a family request, use a known number and a fact only the real person should know.
recovery: Record which independent channel confirmed or rejected the request.
If details were exposed, follow the real provider's recovery process promptly.
Warn affected contacts if your identity or account may have been imitated.
citations: Scamwatch: How to check a scam

articles.title: Keeping security codes private
articles.summary: Understand why one-time codes, PINs and recovery phrases must never be read to an unexpected caller.
articles.overview: A one-time code proves control of an account or payment. A genuine employee should not need you to read back a code that says not to share it, and no support worker needs a recovery phrase.
signs: The caller says the code is needed to cancel fraud or secure the account.
A login notification arrives while someone is speaking with you.
You are asked to move codes between two devices or messaging apps.
actions: Do not read, forward, photograph or type the code into a supplied page.
Close the contact and sign in through the official app to review activity.
Reject unexpected login prompts and change credentials if you approved one.
recovery: Contact the provider's official fraud team and ask it to revoke active sessions.
Change the password and recovery details from a trusted device.
Tell your bank quickly if the code related to a payment or card.

articles.title: Ask a trusted person before acting
articles.summary: Use a second opinion to break isolation, urgency and emotional pressure before money or information moves.
articles.overview: Scammers often insist on secrecy because another person may notice an inconsistency. A calm second opinion is a security control, not an admission that you have made a mistake.
signs: You are told not to involve relatives, bank staff, police or advisers.
The story creates fear, affection or embarrassment that makes checking difficult.
The request changes when another person asks for evidence.
actions: Pause and tell a trusted person exactly what was requested.
Let them verify contact details separately rather than calling the supplied number.
Agree on a family phrase or callback habit for urgent money requests.
recovery: Ask the trusted person to help contact banks and providers through official channels.
Keep evidence together while avoiding further engagement with the requester.
Seek support; being manipulated is not a personal failure.

articles.title: Spotting scam text messages
articles.summary: Recognise parcel, toll, bank and account-alert texts that try to move you to a fake destination.
articles.overview: A scam text may appear in an existing message thread because sender names can be imitated. The wording often creates a small urgent problem, such as a missed delivery or unpaid toll.
signs: The link uses a shortened, misspelled or unrelated domain.
The message asks for a small payment plus card or identity details.
The sender requests a code, password or app installation.
actions: Do not reply or open the supplied link.
Open the organisation's official app or type its known address yourself.
Use Check It only if you deliberately choose to inspect the message or link.
recovery: Contact your bank if card details or a payment were entered.
Change reused passwords and reject unexpected login prompts.
Report the text through your carrier and Scamwatch, then delete it.

articles.title: Spotting phishing email
articles.summary: Check unexpected email without trusting its sender name, buttons or attachments.
articles.overview: Phishing email imitates an organisation to steal sign-in details, money or documents. Display names and logos are easy to copy, so the destination and independent account status matter more than appearance.
signs: The sender address does not match the organisation's normal domain.
A button hides an unrelated destination or unusual spelling.
The message unexpectedly asks for payment changes, credentials or an attachment.
actions: Do not use email buttons; visit the known website or app separately.
Confirm invoices or payment changes by a previously known phone number.
Treat attachments as untrusted unless the sender confirms them through another channel.
recovery: Reset exposed account credentials and revoke sessions.
Tell the organisation if its identity or a staff account may be misused.
Preserve headers and the message for reporting without forwarding it widely.

articles.title: Fake invoices and payment changes
articles.summary: Verify invoices and changed bank details before a business or household payment is redirected.
articles.overview: Invoice fraud may follow a compromised email account or a convincing imitation. Criminals often wait for a real payment conversation, then substitute account details at the last moment.
signs: Bank details change without a previously agreed verification process.
The email requests secrecy or unusually fast payment.
Reply addresses, signatures or writing style differ from earlier correspondence.
actions: Call a known contact using a number already on file, not the invoice.
Read back the account name and details through the independent channel.
Use dual approval for new beneficiaries or changed payment instructions.
recovery: Contact both banks immediately and request a transfer recall.
Secure affected email accounts and inspect forwarding rules.
Report business email compromise to the ACSC and police as appropriate.

articles.title: What makes a link dangerous
articles.summary: Learn how misleading domains, redirects and copied pages can hide the destination of a link.
articles.overview: A link can display familiar words while opening a different destination. Attackers use misspellings, extra subdomains, shortened links and redirects to make a page look connected to a trusted brand.
signs: The important brand name appears before another domain ending.
The address uses unusual spelling, punctuation or a shortened service.
The page immediately asks for credentials, payment or notification permission.
actions: Read the registered domain from right to left before the first slash.
Open the organisation's official app or a saved bookmark instead.
Use Check It for a specific link only when you deliberately request analysis.
recovery: Close the page and clear any permissions you granted.
Change credentials if they were entered and review recent sessions.
Contact your bank if card or transfer information was submitted.

articles.title: Unexpected attachments
articles.summary: Treat surprise documents, archives and installers carefully even when the message appears familiar.
articles.overview: An attachment can carry harmful software or lead to a fake sign-in page. A compromised contact may send a believable file, so familiarity alone does not establish safety.
signs: The file type is unusual for the sender or hidden behind an archive.
A document asks you to enable macros, editing or content.
The message gives little context and pressures you to open the file.
actions: Confirm the file through a known channel before opening it.
Do not enable macros or install software requested by the document.
Keep operating systems and security tools updated before handling expected files.
recovery: Disconnect from sensitive accounts if software unexpectedly ran.
Use the device vendor's official security and recovery guidance.
Notify the sender through another channel because their account may be compromised.

articles.title: Bank impersonation calls
articles.summary: Respond safely when a caller says your money or account is at immediate risk.
articles.overview: A criminal may spoof the bank's number, know personal details, and describe a fake fraud emergency. They may ask you to move money to a safe account or reveal a security code.
signs: The caller asks for a one-time code or full online banking password.
You are told to transfer money to protect it.
The caller insists you remain on the line while taking action.
actions: Hang up and call the bank using the number on your card or official app.
Never transfer money to a safe account named by an incoming caller.
Review account alerts only after reaching the bank independently.
recovery: Tell the bank's fraud team immediately about any transfer or code shared.
Ask it to freeze affected access and recall payments where possible.
Report the impersonation to Scamwatch and police if money was lost.

articles.title: Government impersonation
articles.summary: Recognise threats about tax, police, immigration or benefits that misuse official names and authority.
articles.overview: Government impersonation uses fear of arrest, debt or lost benefits. Australian agencies do not demand immediate secrecy or payment through gift cards, cryptocurrency or an unexpected personal account.
signs: The caller threatens arrest or deportation unless payment is immediate.
Payment is requested by gift card, cryptocurrency or money transfer.
The caller refuses to provide a reference that can be checked independently.
actions: End the call and locate the agency's official contact page yourself.
Ask the agency whether the reference and claim exist.
Do not provide identity documents or remote access during an incoming call.
recovery: Contact your bank if money or payment details were provided.
Use official identity recovery services if documents were disclosed.
Report the event to Scamwatch and the impersonated agency.

articles.title: Remote-access support scams
articles.summary: Know why an unexpected caller should never control your phone or computer.
articles.overview: A caller may claim to be from a technology company, bank or telecommunications provider and ask you to install remote-control software. That access can expose accounts and approve payments.
signs: Support contacts you unexpectedly about an unseen problem.
You are asked to install AnyDesk, TeamViewer or another control app.
The caller asks you to hide the screen from bank staff or relatives.
actions: Do not install software or grant accessibility and screen-sharing permissions.
Hang up and contact the organisation through its official support channel.
Remove unknown apps and review permissions if installation began.
recovery: Disconnect the device from networks if remote control may still be active.
Contact banks from a different trusted device and secure accounts.
Seek official technical help to remove software and review the device.

articles.title: Caller ID can be copied
articles.summary: Understand why a familiar number or sender name does not prove who is calling.
articles.overview: Caller ID information can be altered so an incoming call appears to use a bank, agency or local number. The number shown on screen is therefore only a clue, not identity proof.
signs: The caller relies on the displayed number as proof.
They object when you say you will call back independently.
They request codes, payments or remote access during the incoming call.
actions: Hang up and wait briefly before placing a new call.
Dial a number from an official app, statement or trusted website.
Ask the real organisation to check whether it attempted contact.
recovery: Block the number only as a nuisance control; spoofers can change numbers.
Secure accounts if private details were shared.
Report repeated impersonation with times and claimed organisations.

articles.title: Family emergency impersonation
articles.summary: Verify urgent money requests that appear to come from a child, grandchild or friend.
articles.overview: A scammer may imitate a relative's voice, use a stolen account or claim the person's phone has changed. The story often includes an accident, arrest or lost device and asks for secrecy.
signs: The contact uses a new number and cannot answer normal family questions.
You are told not to contact parents, partners or other relatives.
Payment is requested through gift cards, cryptocurrency or a third party.
actions: Call the person on their known number and contact another family member.
Use a family safe phrase or ask a question not visible online.
Do not send money until the situation is independently confirmed.
recovery: Contact the payment provider quickly if money was sent.
Warn the real person and family that their identity is being used.
Review social accounts for exposed family details and tighten privacy.

articles.title: Fake online stores
articles.summary: Check whether an online shop is genuine before entering payment or identity details.
articles.overview: Fake stores copy product photos, reviews and branding, then disappear or misuse card details. A polished site and paid advertisement are not proof of a real business.
signs: Prices are far below other sellers and the discount expires quickly.
Contact, returns and business information cannot be verified.
Only irreversible payment methods are accepted.
actions: Search the business name, ABN, address and independent reviews separately.
Read delivery and return terms before paying.
Use a card or payment service with dispute protection rather than a transfer.
recovery: Contact the card issuer to dispute unauthorised or undelivered purchases.
Change a reused password and monitor the card for further charges.
Report the store and advertisement to Scamwatch and the platform.

articles.title: Online marketplace scams
articles.summary: Deal more safely with buyers, sellers, courier claims and payment links on marketplace platforms.
articles.overview: Marketplace scammers may pose as buyers or sellers, send fake payment confirmations, or move the conversation outside the platform. They exploit urgency around collection and delivery.
signs: A buyer sends a courier story and asks you to pay a fee first.
A seller refuses platform protections or inspection.
A payment email or screenshot is the only proof of funds.
actions: Keep communication and payment inside the platform where possible.
Confirm cleared funds in your own account, not through a supplied link.
Meet in a safe public place and inspect high-value items.
recovery: Report the account and conversation to the marketplace.
Contact your payment provider if funds or card details were exposed.
Keep listing, profile and payment evidence for reporting.

articles.title: Investment scams
articles.summary: Question high returns, celebrity claims and private investment groups before transferring money.
articles.overview: Investment scams use professional websites, fake trading dashboards and social proof. Early withdrawals may be allowed to build trust before larger deposits are requested.
signs: Returns are guaranteed or described as low risk and unusually high.
A private chat group or celebrity image replaces licensed advice.
Extra tax or release fees are demanded before withdrawal.
actions: Check the provider and adviser through ASIC registers and investor alerts.
Do not install trading software supplied by an unsolicited contact.
Seek independent licensed advice before moving retirement savings.
recovery: Stop sending further fees, even when promised recovery.
Contact banks and exchanges promptly with transaction details.
Report to ASIC, Scamwatch and police, and beware follow-up recovery scams.

articles.title: Romance and friendship payment requests
articles.summary: Recognise when an online relationship is being used to create repeated financial pressure.
articles.overview: Romance scammers invest time in trust and emotional intimacy before introducing travel, medical, legal or investment emergencies. They may avoid live meetings and use stolen photographs.
signs: Plans to meet repeatedly fail because of a new crisis.
Money is requested through transfers, gift cards or cryptocurrency.
The person discourages discussion with friends or family.
actions: Pause all payments and discuss the relationship with someone you trust.
Reverse-image search profile photos and verify claims independently.
Do not receive or move money for the person.
recovery: Contact your bank and report accounts or transfers.
Preserve conversations while ending financial contact.
Seek confidential support; emotional manipulation can affect anyone.

articles.title: Gift card and cryptocurrency demands
articles.summary: Treat demands for irreversible payment methods as a serious warning sign.
articles.overview: Gift cards and cryptocurrency can be transferred quickly and are difficult to reverse. Legitimate government agencies, banks and service providers do not use them to settle surprise debts or secure accounts.
signs: You are told exactly which cards to buy and to read out the numbers.
A caller stays on the line while you visit a shop or exchange.
The payment is described as tax, bail, technical support or account protection.
actions: Stop before purchasing or transferring anything.
Verify the claim through the organisation's official channel.
Tell shop staff or your bank that someone instructed you to make the payment.
recovery: Contact the gift card issuer or exchange immediately.
Save wallet addresses, receipts and messages for investigators.
Report the demand to Scamwatch and police if money was lost.

articles.title: Unexpected account alerts
articles.summary: Check login, password-reset and recovery warnings without using the message link.
articles.overview: Some alerts are genuine and some are phishing. The safest response is the same: avoid the supplied link and inspect the account directly through its official app or known website.
signs: The alert creates urgency but provides vague device or location details.
The sender domain or destination differs from the provider's official domain.
A supposed support agent contacts you immediately after the alert.
actions: Open the official app independently and review recent sessions.
Reject login prompts you did not initiate.
Change the password and recovery details if activity is unfamiliar.
recovery: Sign out other sessions and enable strong multi-factor authentication.
Check forwarding rules and recovery contacts for unauthorised changes.
Contact official support if access is lost.

articles.title: What to do about a reused password
articles.summary: Use a practical order for changing important accounts after one password is exposed.
articles.overview: When the same password is used in several places, one breach can lead to automated attempts elsewhere. Start with accounts that control money, email and password recovery.
signs: You receive login alerts from several services after one breach.
An old password appears in a breach notice or extortion message.
Recovery emails or forwarding rules change unexpectedly.
actions: Change the primary email password first, then banking and other important accounts.
Use a unique password generated and stored by a reputable password manager.
Enable multi-factor authentication that does not rely only on SMS where available.
recovery: Revoke active sessions and remove unknown recovery methods.
Check financial and email activity for changes made before the reset.
Monitor official breach notices without paying an extortion demand.

articles.title: Protecting identity documents
articles.summary: Limit copies of licences, passports and identity numbers and respond if they are exposed.
articles.overview: Identity documents can support account opening and impersonation long after a single scam. Organisations should explain why a document is required, how it is protected and whether a less sensitive option exists.
signs: A new contact requests multiple documents before basic verification.
Documents must be sent through personal email or an unfamiliar upload page.
The requester cannot explain retention or deletion.
actions: Verify the organisation and purpose independently before sharing.
Provide only the required fields and use approved secure channels.
Add a dated watermark where the receiving process permits it.
recovery: Contact the issuing authority and identity support services.
Monitor credit activity and accounts opened in your name.
Keep records of what was shared, when and with whom.

articles.title: Phone number and SIM takeover
articles.summary: Recognise warning signs when calls or messages stop and accounts begin requesting recovery.
articles.overview: A SIM takeover moves your number to another SIM or service, allowing an attacker to receive calls and SMS codes. Loss of service without explanation can be an early sign.
signs: The phone suddenly shows no service while others nearby are connected.
The carrier reports a SIM or account change you did not request.
Password-reset or banking alerts appear around the same time.
actions: Contact the carrier through its official number using another phone.
Ask it to lock the account and reverse unauthorised changes.
Contact banks and primary email providers immediately.
recovery: Replace SMS-only authentication where stronger options exist.
Add a carrier account PIN and review authorised contacts.
Document affected accounts and report identity misuse.

articles.title: Use official account recovery
articles.summary: Avoid fake recovery services and sponsored impostor results when regaining an account.
articles.overview: Attackers advertise fake support numbers and recovery services, especially after a person has already lost access or money. Search placement does not prove that a result belongs to the provider.
signs: Support asks for payment, gift cards or remote access before helping.
The contact address uses a generic email or messaging account.
The service promises guaranteed recovery of cryptocurrency or funds.
actions: Start from the provider's official app or typed website.
Use documented recovery forms and keep reference numbers.
Do not share passwords, one-time codes or recovery phrases with support.
recovery: Report impostor advertisements to the platform and provider.
Secure related email and payment accounts.
Treat unsolicited recovery offers as a new scam attempt.

articles.title: Unsafe app permissions
articles.summary: Question requests for access to messages, accessibility, microphone, contacts and device control.
articles.overview: Permissions let an app use sensitive device functions. A legitimate app should request only what its feature needs and explain the purpose at the moment of use.
signs: A simple app requests accessibility, SMS or device-administrator access.
Permission prompts appear before any related feature is used.
The app came from a link or unofficial store.
actions: Deny unexpected access and review the app's official store listing.
Open system settings to remove permissions you no longer need.
Uninstall apps that cannot justify sensitive access.
recovery: Change important credentials if an app could observe them.
Review banking, messages and account sessions for misuse.
Use the device vendor's official malware and recovery guidance.

articles.title: Fake security and cleaner apps
articles.summary: Avoid apps chosen by alarming pop-ups, scareware messages or unsolicited support contacts.
articles.overview: A browser warning may claim the device is infected and direct you to install a cleaner or security app. Websites cannot normally diagnose the whole device in this way.
signs: A countdown or loud alert says damage is happening now.
The install link bypasses the official app store.
The app demands broad permissions, subscriptions or remote control.
actions: Close the browser tab without using its buttons.
Check device security through system settings or the vendor's official support.
Install software only from the official store after independent review.
recovery: Remove the app and revoke its permissions or profiles.
Cancel unwanted subscriptions through the official store.
Secure accounts if the app could read screens, messages or credentials.

articles.title: Using public Wi-Fi more safely
articles.summary: Know when to switch to mobile data and avoid sensitive activity on an unfamiliar network.
articles.overview: Public Wi-Fi can be useful, but network names may be copied and some networks capture browsing through sign-in pages. Modern encrypted websites help, but the network itself is not proof of trust.
signs: Several networks use nearly identical names.
The sign-in page asks for unrelated identity or payment details.
The device warns that the network or certificate is insecure.
actions: Confirm the correct network name with staff.
Use mobile data for banking, account recovery or sensitive work.
Forget the network after use and disable automatic joining.
recovery: Change credentials if you entered them after a certificate warning.
Review account sessions and payment activity.
Remove unknown VPN, profile or certificate settings.

articles.title: QR code scams
articles.summary: Check where a printed or emailed QR code leads before signing in or paying.
articles.overview: A QR code is simply another way to encode a link or other data. Stickers can cover legitimate codes on parking meters, menus or posters, and email codes can lead to phishing pages.
signs: A sticker appears placed over the original code.
The opened domain does not match the service or payment provider.
The page asks for unusual credentials, app installation or a transfer.
actions: Inspect the physical code and preview the destination before opening it.
Use the service's official app or typed address for payment.
Do not grant notifications, profiles or downloads from the destination.
recovery: Contact the card issuer if payment details were entered.
Change credentials used on the page and revoke sessions.
Tell the venue or organisation so the code can be removed.

articles.title: Unexpected device warnings
articles.summary: Separate genuine system settings from scareware, browser pop-ups and fake support messages.
articles.overview: Real operating-system warnings appear through known system interfaces and settings. A web page can imitate those colours and icons but cannot reliably scan the entire device.
signs: The warning includes a phone number to call immediately.
Closing it opens more windows or prevents normal navigation.
It requests payment, remote access or installation of a cleaner.
actions: Close the browser or app through the normal system controls.
Open device security and update settings directly.
Contact the manufacturer through its official support page if unsure.
recovery: Remove software or profiles installed because of the warning.
Secure accounts accessed while remote control was active.
Contact banks if the caller observed or directed financial activity.

articles.title: Contact your bank after a scam
articles.summary: Act quickly with clear information when money, card details or online banking may be affected.
articles.overview: Banks may be able to stop cards, secure access, recall transfers or begin a dispute. Speed matters, but use only the number on your card, statement or official banking app.
signs: An unauthorised payment or new beneficiary appears.
You sent money after deception or shared a security code.
A caller viewed or controlled your banking session.
actions: Call the bank's fraud team and explain exactly what happened.
Provide transaction times, amounts and recipient details.
Ask which accounts, cards, sessions and devices need securing.
recovery: Follow the bank's written case process and keep reference numbers.
Monitor accounts and credit for further misuse.
Report the scam to Scamwatch and police where appropriate.

articles.title: Secure important accounts
articles.summary: Follow a calm order for passwords, sessions, recovery details and multi-factor security after an incident.
articles.overview: Start with accounts that can reset others: primary email, mobile service and password manager. Then protect banking, government and social accounts without reusing a compromised password.
signs: Recovery details, forwarding rules or sessions changed unexpectedly.
Several accounts report logins from unfamiliar devices.
Contacts receive messages you did not send.
actions: Use a trusted device and secure the primary email first.
Change each affected password to a unique value and revoke sessions.
Replace unknown recovery methods and enable strong multi-factor authentication.
recovery: Tell contacts to ignore suspicious messages from your account.
Record support case numbers and recovery dates.
Continue monitoring because attackers may retry older credentials.

articles.title: Keep useful evidence safely
articles.summary: Retain the information banks, platforms and investigators may need without continuing contact.
articles.overview: Useful evidence explains what happened and where money or accounts moved. Preserve it safely, but do not keep harmful files open or continue a conversation merely to collect more.
signs: Messages, receipts or account names may disappear when blocked.
Different platforms hold separate parts of the conversation.
Sensitive identity or banking data is mixed with useful evidence.
actions: Save screenshots, dates, usernames, transaction references and URLs.
Store copies in a trusted location and redact secrets before sharing widely.
Do not reopen attachments or revisit unsafe links for evidence.
recovery: Give each organisation only the evidence relevant to its process.
Keep a timeline of reports, reference numbers and actions.
Delete extra sensitive copies when the legitimate process is complete.

articles.title: Where to report a scam
articles.summary: Choose the relevant official channel for money loss, cybercrime, harmful content and identity misuse.
articles.overview: Reporting does not guarantee recovery, but it can support bank action, platform removal and wider warnings. Different organisations handle payments, cybercrime, identity and immediate danger.
signs: Money, identity documents, accounts or devices may be affected.
The same scam is reaching other people or using a public advertisement.
Threats or immediate physical danger are involved.
actions: Contact the bank or provider first when urgent containment is possible.
Report scam details to Scamwatch and cybercrime through ReportCyber.
Call Triple Zero for immediate danger, not for routine online reporting.
recovery: Keep report references and follow official requests for evidence.
Report accounts or advertisements to the platform as well.
Ignore unsolicited people who promise recovery for an upfront fee.

articles.title: Recovering confidence after a scam
articles.summary: Rebuild safer habits without blame after manipulation, loss or a close call.
articles.overview: Scams are designed and tested to manipulate ordinary human reactions. Shame can delay practical help, while a calm review can turn the experience into a small number of useful habits.
signs: You avoid checking accounts because the situation feels overwhelming.
You blame yourself more than you review the scammer's tactics.
Follow-up recovery contacts promise certainty or pressure you again.
actions: Tell a trusted person and complete urgent bank or account steps together.
Write down the warning signs that mattered in this incident.
Adopt one or two repeatable checks rather than trying to distrust everything.
recovery: Use confidential financial, identity or counselling support if needed.
Block and report follow-up recovery scammers.
Review progress after a week and keep protective changes that help.

articles.title: Job and recruitment scams
articles.summary: Check unexpected job offers, equipment payments and requests for identity documents.
articles.overview: Fake recruiters advertise flexible, high-paid work and may conduct interviews only through messaging apps. They seek upfront payments, money movement or identity documents rather than legitimate employment.
signs: The role is offered without a normal interview or verifiable employer email.
You must pay for training, equipment or a background check.
The work involves receiving and forwarding money or parcels.
actions: Verify the vacancy on the employer's official careers page.
Call the organisation through its published switchboard.
Do not use your bank account to process employer or customer funds.
recovery: Contact your bank and identity support services if details were shared.
Report the advertisement to the platform and Scamwatch.
Preserve offer letters, profiles and payment instructions.

articles.title: Charity and donation scams
articles.summary: Verify urgent donation requests after disasters, emergencies and community events.
articles.overview: Scammers exploit public concern after disasters or personal tragedies. They may copy a charity's name, create a fake fundraising page or approach people directly with unverifiable stories.
signs: The collector cannot provide the charity's registered details.
The payment goes to a personal account or unusual method.
The appeal uses pressure and discourages independent checking.
actions: Search the charity register and donate through the official site.
Check crowdfunding organisers and beneficiaries separately.
Avoid entering card details through a link in an unsolicited message.
recovery: Ask the payment provider about disputing a fraudulent donation.
Report the page to its host and the copied charity.
Report the scam to Scamwatch with the fundraiser URL.

articles.title: Rental and accommodation scams
articles.summary: Check properties, agents and payment demands before sending a bond or deposit.
articles.overview: A scammer may copy a real listing, claim to be overseas, and demand a deposit before inspection. Short-term accommodation scams can similarly use copied photos and false booking pages.
signs: The price is unusually low and inspection is impossible.
Money is requested before a lease, identity check or verified viewing.
The account name does not match the agent or owner.
actions: Inspect the property or use a trusted representative.
Verify the agent's licence and office through independent records.
Read the lease and use the authorised bond process for your state.
recovery: Contact the bank immediately if a deposit was sent.
Report copied listings to the platform and real agent.
Report the fraud to police and Scamwatch with account details.

articles.title: Subscription traps and hidden renewals
articles.summary: Read trial, renewal and cancellation terms before entering card details.
articles.overview: A low-cost trial can become a recurring charge when terms are hidden or cancellation is deliberately difficult. Scam advertisements may also imitate a known brand or survey.
signs: The ongoing price is separated from the prominent trial offer.
Cancellation requires contacting an unrelated address or giving more data.
Small unfamiliar charges appear before larger renewals.
actions: Read total price, renewal date and cancellation method before paying.
Use a payment method with transaction controls and statements.
Keep confirmation and cancellation records.
recovery: Cancel through the legitimate merchant process and keep proof.
Ask the card issuer about charge disputes and merchant blocks.
Replace the card if unauthorised charging continues.

articles.title: Social media account takeover
articles.summary: Respond when a friend's profile or your own account starts sending unusual requests.
articles.overview: A compromised social account can exploit existing trust, advertise fake investments, or ask contacts for codes and money. The profile history may look genuine because it belongs to a real person.
signs: The writing style or request differs from normal conversations.
The account asks for a code sent to your phone.
A new investment or emergency story appears across several contacts.
actions: Contact the person through another known channel.
Do not send codes, money or account-recovery links.
Report the compromised profile through the platform.
recovery: Use official recovery, revoke sessions and replace recovery details.
Warn contacts and remove fraudulent posts or messages.
Secure the associated email account before restoring social access.

articles.title: Online blackmail and sextortion
articles.summary: Take safe steps when someone threatens to share intimate material or demands money.
articles.overview: Sextortion uses threats, shame and urgency to demand money or more material. Paying rarely guarantees the threats will stop and may lead to repeated demands.
signs: A new contact quickly moves toward intimate conversation or images.
The person claims to have recorded you and demands secrecy.
Payment or more material is required under a short deadline.
actions: Stop contact, do not pay and preserve messages and account details.
Tighten account privacy and block the person after evidence is saved.
Report image-based abuse to eSafety and threats to police.
recovery: Tell a trusted person so you are not handling the pressure alone.
Use platform reporting and eSafety removal pathways.
If a child is involved or anyone is in immediate danger, contact police promptly.

articles.title: Deepfake voice and video requests
articles.summary: Verify urgent requests even when a voice or video appears to show someone you know.
articles.overview: Artificially generated or edited audio and video can imitate a person's appearance or voice. A short familiar-sounding clip should not replace an independent callback or family verification habit.
signs: The call is brief, urgent and avoids normal conversation.
The person cannot answer a private shared question.
Money must be sent to a new account or unusual payment method.
actions: End the call and contact the person through a known channel.
Use a family safe phrase that is not posted online.
Confirm money requests with another trusted relative or colleague.
recovery: Contact the payment provider if money was sent.
Warn the impersonated person and likely targets.
Save the media and report the account without redistributing it.

articles.title: Responding to a data breach notice
articles.summary: Confirm the notice, understand what data was involved and take proportionate recovery steps.
articles.overview: A genuine breach notice should identify the organisation, affected information and recommended steps. Criminals also imitate breach notices to collect more data, so confirm it independently.
signs: The notice asks you to sign in through an unexpected link.
It requests passwords, codes or payment to protect your data.
The organisation has no matching notice on its official channels.
actions: Visit the organisation's official site or call a known number.
Change exposed or reused credentials and review account sessions.
Follow specific advice for identity, financial or health information.
recovery: Monitor relevant accounts and credit activity.
Keep the confirmed notice for later identity-recovery processes.
Be alert for targeted follow-up scams using the exposed details.
